summary: Defines an OSPFv3-based auto-discovery mechanism for Layer 1 VPNs. It parallels the existing OSPF version 2 mechanism, with support for IPv6 as the notable difference. It is an Experimental protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: Private links need to find each other automatically. This note gives a way for routers using the newer addressing to discover those links on their own, copying an older way that only worked with the old addressing.

questions: how does l1vpn discovery work with ipv6
subtitle: Using OSPFv3 to discover Layer 1 VPN connections with IPv6 support.

tldr.problem: Layer 1 VPNs need to map customer port identifiers to provider port identifiers automatically. A parallel mechanism exists for OSPFv2, but it does not support IPv6.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a new OSPFv3 Link State Advertisement (LSA) type and a corresponding TLV for advertising L1VPN membership and port mapping information. PEs use OSPFv3 to flood this information across the network.
tldr.outcome: Networks can auto-discover L1VPN connections using the newer OSPFv3 protocol with native IPv6 support, mirroring the OSPFv2-based discovery mechanism.

today: RFC 5523 is an Experimental protocol. It extends OSPFv3 to support Layer 1 VPN auto-discovery with IPv6. This document parallels RFC 5252 (the OSPFv2 version) and is used by providers deploying modern IPv6-native networks for customer VPN services.

sections.title: Layer 1 VPN Auto-Discovery
sections.content:
A Layer 1 Virtual Private Network (L1VPN) lets a service provider offer isolated virtual circuits to customers over a shared physical infrastructure. To set up a connection, the provider must map each customer's port identifier (CPI) to the provider's port identifier (PPI) and maintain a Port Information Table (PIT) at each edge router.

This mapping information can be manually configured or automatically discovered. RFC 5252 defines an OSPFv2-based auto-discovery mechanism. This document provides the same functionality using OSPFv3 (OSPF for IPv6), which is notably different in its support for IPv6 addresses and link-local identifiers.

The two mechanisms are parallel: the same concepts and procedures apply, but OSPFv3's native IPv6 support allows modern deployments to avoid IPv4 altogether.
sections.plainLanguage: A service provider has routers connecting different customers. Those routers need to tell each other which customer port connects to which provider port. This document shows how routers using IPv6 can share that information automatically.

sections.title: The OSPFv3 L1VPN LSA and TLVs
sections.content:
This RFC introduces a new OSPFv3 L1VPN LSA (Link State Advertisement) with LSA Function Code 14. The LSA carries L1VPN discovery information in TLV (Type-Length-Value) format. At minimum, it contains one L1VPN Info TLV; it may optionally contain a TE Link TLV for traffic engineering attributes.

The L1VPN IPv6 Info TLV (type 32768) is the key new TLV defined here. It contains a globally unique L1VPN identifier, the provider edge router's TE address, a link-local identifier (for unnumbered links), and the auto-discovery information (CPI to PPI mappings).

The LSA structure follows standard OSPFv3 conventions, with standard fields like LS age, sequence number, and checksum. Area or AS flooding scope is determined by configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router sends an advertisement listing which customer ports it has and where they connect to. The advertisement is wrapped in a message format OSPFv3 routers understand.

sections.title: Advertising and Processing
sections.content:
Each PE (Provider Edge) router originates one OSPFv3 L1VPN LSA for each local customer edge (CE) link, either on restart or whenever the PIT entry changes. The LSA is flooded according to OSPFv3 rules (area or AS scope).

When a PE receives a new, removed, or modified L1VPN LSA, it checks whether the L1VPN Globally Unique Identifier matches any L1VPN it supports locally. If so, it updates its PIT accordingly: adding, removing, or modifying entries based on the advertised port mappings. In steady state, all PEs supporting the same L1VPN end up with identical local PITs, enabling consistent routing of customer traffic.

If the LSA contains more than one L1VPN Info TLV or TE Link TLV, receiving PEs SHOULD ignore all but the first of each type. If an LSA has no L1VPN Info TLV, it is processed as normal OSPF but does not modify any PITs.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router says: 'I have a link from customer port X to provider port Y.' Other routers listen and update their tables so they know where to send traffic.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility and Migration
sections.content:
The OSPFv3 L1VPN LSA introduces no interoperability issues. Per RFC 5340, because the U-bit in the LS type is set, OSPFv3 speakers that do not support the L1VPN LSA simply participate in its flooding but ignore its contents. This ensures safe coexistence with non-L1VPN-aware routers.

Migration from OSPFv2-based L1VPN discovery to OSPFv3 is a one-time event tied to the network's migration to OSPFv3 for other routing purposes. A suggested sequence involves assigning IPv6 addresses, installing OSPFv3, advertising resources with both protocols during a transition period, then cutting over to OSPFv3 and disabling OSPFv2.
sections.plainLanguage: Old routers that don't understand this new message type will just pass it along without breaking. Switching from the old IPv4 method to the new IPv6 method is a planned migration, not an immediate cutover.

sections.title: Security and Manageability
sections.content:
The security considerations for OSPFv3 L1VPN discovery are the same as those for OSPFv3 itself (RFC 5340). OSPF provides authentication (multiple types), rate limiting of LSA origination, and database overflow protection. For end-to-end LSA authentication, operators can use mechanisms similar to RFC 2154 (OSPF with Digital Signatures).

From a management perspective, each PE must be configured with the L1VPNs it supports, typically tied to the configuration of its customer-facing ports and the PITs they establish. Implementations may expose learned L1VPN membership via the OSPFv3 MIB or Traffic Engineering Database MIB. The control plane has no impact on Layer 1 user data because all traffic is in Layer 1 while the control plane is out-of-band.
sections.plainLanguage: OSPF already has security features like passwords. Routers must know which L1VPNs they belong to, but that can be automatically matched to the ports they connect to.
